issues.issue: The fall-back definitional hierarchy ("in the Policy described below or, if not defined therein, in the Indenture") plus the opening qualifier "[u]nless the context clearly requires otherwise" leaves it open which source governs a term used in more than one instrument. The qualifier itself invites argument about when context "clearly" displaces the stated order.
"Commission" and "SEC" are separately defined to mean the same body, and the operative text uses both, leaving a needless duplication to reconcile.

The definition is purely a cross-reference and the citation is garbled ("Section 2.02(c)(ill)"), so the referent must be reconstructed. The intended target, Section 2.02(c)(iii), is nonetheless identifiable.

The definition opens an enumeration with "(i)" that has no "(ii)", so it is unclear whether an intended second limb of the Financial Statements definition was dropped. The omission matters because Section 2.01(h) makes representations about the completeness of these statements.

"[T]he first January 31 to occur thereafter" does not say what it is measured from — the No Form 15D Notice or the stated January 31, 2008 — so the termination date can be read as a rolling or a single date. The whole conditional structure (notice that "no Form 15D will be filed") is hard to apply.

The cross-reference is wrong: "Insurer Financial Statements" is actually defined in Section 2.05(l), not in "Section 2.03()", which is the negative-covenants section and contains no such term. A reader must supply the correct section for the definition to work at all.

The term is defined only by cross-reference to Section 3.04(a)(v), a subsection of the indemnification article, while the operative representation about Insurer Information sits in Section 2.05(e); the scope of the defined term must be imported from elsewhere. If the citation is inaccurate the term has no content at all.

"Material Adverse Change" is defined in terms of a "material adverse change ... which might have such effect" — "might" and "material" set no measurable boundary, and the term conditions a large number of covenants and representations throughout Articles II and V. Parties can reasonably differ on whether any given change qualifies.

After listing three specific documents the definition sweeps in "any other offering document in respect of the Securities prepared by or on behalf of the Depositor that makes reference to the Policy," leaving the reach of the catch-all uncertain. The representations in Section 2.01(m) turn on which documents fall inside it.

The enumerated list of agreements is followed by the catch-all "each other document contemplated by any of the foregoing to which the Depositor, the Owner Trustee, the Master Servicer, the Servicer, the Indenture Trustee or the Trust is a party," whose reach is undefined. Because nearly every covenant in Article II is keyed to "Operative Documents," the catch-all's scope has real operative consequences.

The definition is framed around "Mortgage Loan," a term this Agreement does not itself define and which sits alongside the Agreement's usual term "HELOCs." Whether Originators relates to all HELOCs or only some loans is left to inference.

The definition makes Premium payable "in accordance with this Insurance Agreement," "pursuant to the Premium Letter" and "in accordance with the Indenture" at once, without saying which controls if they differ; Section 3.02(c) repeats the same triple reference.

The clause is drafted as both a present representation and a forward promise — "is, or shall become, duly qualified" and "has obtained, or shall obtain, all necessary licenses" — so it is unclear whether a failure to be qualified at closing is a breach at all. The qualifier "in each jurisdiction in which the failure ... would render any Operative Document unenforceable in any respect" further blurs the boundary.

The Section 2.01 chapeau states the representations are given "as of the Closing Date" and Section 3.01(c) makes their truth on the Closing Date a condition, which cannot easily be squared with a representation that qualification may occur later ("shall become").

The no-default representation is given only by "EMC [and] the Depositor" while the same subsection's second sentence and the rest of Section 2.01 are given by EMC, the Issuer and the Depositor, leaving the Issuer's position unstated. Whether the omission is deliberate is a live question.

A perpetual promise never to "deny" the validity of the Operative Documents sits inside a section of closing-date representations; whether it operates as an estoppel, a waiver of defences, or merely a warranty is unclear. Its reach against defences such as fraud or illegality is not addressed.

"[H]ave a material possibility of causing a Material Adverse Change" states a threshold of likelihood that has no settled meaning and no benchmark in the Agreement. The phrase compounds two vague standards, "material possibility" and "Material Adverse Change."

The representation that the Issuer holds the Collateral "free and clear of all liens" is hard to reconcile with Section 2.01(q), which provides that on the Closing Date the Indenture Trustee shall have a first perfected priority interest in the same collateral.

"Documents" is defined to include the Operative Documents plus the open-ended category of "other material information relating to the HELOCs, the operations of EMC, the Issuer or the Depositor or the financial condition of" those parties, so the boundary of the accuracy representation is set by a general catch-all rather than any list. Whether loan-level tapes, models or diligence materials fall inside it is left open.

The unqualified representation that "the information in the Data Tape with respect to each HELOC is true and correct" is not limited by materiality or knowledge, unlike the sentences it purports to amplify, so its relationship to the surrounding materiality-qualified representation is contestable. What counts as "information in the Data Tape" — raw fields only, or derived characteristics such as LTV and FICO — is also unstated.

The tape is required by Section 2.02(c)(iii) only to be delivered "on or before the Closing Date," yet accuracy is warranted as of the earlier Cut-off Date of February 15, 2007, leaving the interval unaddressed.

"[C]omplies or shall comply" mixes a present representation with a future undertaking without saying which applies when, so a breach date cannot be fixed from the words. The disjunctive also lets each side pick the reading that suits it.

The proviso carves out "the Servicer Information or the Underwriter Information," but "Underwriter Information" is nowhere defined in this Agreement, so the scope of the exclusion from the disclosure representation is indeterminate. The carve-out list also mixes caption-based exclusions with defined-term exclusions.

"Offered Notes" is used without definition in this Agreement, which elsewhere defines only "Notes" and "Insured Notes," leaving the class of securities covered by the representation uncertain. The pairing with "the Class B-2 Notes" implies the Offered Notes are something narrower than all Notes, but the text does not say what.

The representation is prefaced "Based upon advice of legal counsel," which may either qualify the warranty to a matter of belief or leave it absolute. That qualifier is uniquely attached to this representation and its effect is unexplained.

Wholesale importation of the representations in every Operative Document "as if the same were set forth in full herein" for the Insurer's benefit sits uneasily with Section 2.02(n), which channels breaches of the Depositor Purchase Agreement representations into the remedies of Section 7 of that agreement.

This sentence duplicates verbatim the last sentence of Section 2.01(g), so the same undertaking appears twice with different surrounding qualifications, raising the question whether one of them was meant to be narrower.

The sentence states the consideration received "by the Depositor upon the transfer of the HELOCs to the Trust," but under the recited structure it is the Depositor that transfers to the Trust and the Issuer that pays, so the party receiving value may be misidentified. The reasonably-equivalent-value representation depends on getting the direction of the transfer right.

The subsection is headed "Security Interest in the Loans" but promises a "first perfected priority interest in the collateral," a lower-case term that is not defined in this Agreement, so the property covered is uncertain. The future-tense "shall have" also makes it unclear whether this is a representation or a covenant.
It is difficult to reconcile the Indenture Trustee's first priority interest with Section 2.01(j), which represents that the Issuer holds the Collateral free and clear of all liens.

The covenant to perform under the Operative Documents is limited to "all cases in which failure to so comply or perform would result in a default thereunder," so a breach that does not itself ripen into a default under another agreement may not breach this one. That qualifier substantially narrows an apparently broad compliance covenant.

The quarterly-statement trigger is internally muddled: statements are due "[i]mmediately following the earlier to occur of" a Material Adverse Change or "upon the request of the Insurer", "but in any event within 45 days," so the deadline and the triggering event are stated in two inconsistent ways. The enumerated Data Tape field list closing with "any other information reasonably requested by the Insurer" similarly leaves the required scope open.

The proviso permits website delivery of information "required to be furnished pursuant to Section 2.02(d)(iii)(B)," but Section 2.02(d)(iii) has no clause (B); the intended target is Section 2.02(c)(iii)(B), which the same sentence has just described. The mis-citation changes which information may be posted rather than delivered.

The trigger list is ungrammatical and its connectives are inconsistent — "Once in each calendar year, or at any time following any [Ratings Event], following the occurrence of any Default ..., at any time that the Overcollateralization Target Amount has not been reduced ..., and with respect to the Servicer, an Event of Servicer Termination has occurred" — so it cannot be told whether the listed events are alternatives, cumulative conditions, or an annual cap with exceptions. The Insurer's right of access turns entirely on which reading prevails.

The once-a-year, trigger-conditioned access right is hard to square with the closing paragraph of the same Section 2.02(d), which gives the Insurer an unconditional right to conduct an "ongoing review" of the Servicer's practices through reviews of the HELOCs so long as any Notes are outstanding.

"[O]ngoing review of the Servicer's practices as a Servicer through reviews of the HELOCs, reappraisals of Mortgaged Properties and reviews of servicing practices" does not say what the Insurer may demand — loan files, underwriting documents, or only servicing records — nor at whose cost or on what notice. The word "review" carries a broad and a narrow reading, and the enumerated methods do not fix its limit.

This unconditional, open-ended right introduced by "Notwithstanding the foregoing" is difficult to reconcile with the opening of Section 2.02(d), which limits inspections to once per calendar year absent enumerated triggers and requires a "reasonable request" of the Insurer.

Cost-shifting is expressed as "at the expense of EMC or the Servicer, as applicable," without any rule for deciding which party bears it or how a joint review is apportioned. "[A]ny such undertaking following a Ratings Event" also leaves the temporal reach of the shift unstated.

The cost allocation applies to "the inspections, discussions and due diligence referred to in this Section 2.02(d)," which may or may not capture the separate "ongoing review" right created by the immediately preceding "Notwithstanding the foregoing" paragraph.

The covenant begins with the bare pronoun "It" and never identifies the covenantor, so the obligor must be supplied from the Section 2.02 chapeau. The prohibition on using "any information relating to the Insurer" is also unbounded — publicly available information appears to be caught.

The broad grant that the Insurer "shall have all rights provided to the Insurer in the Operative Documents" as a third-party beneficiary is cut back by the very next sentence of Section 2.02(j), which confines its third-party beneficiary rights under the Indenture; the interaction of the grant and the limit is not spelled out.

Limiting the Insurer to "the rights granted to it and to the Noteholders in the Indenture" is ambiguous as to whether the Insurer may exercise Noteholder rights or only rights expressly granted to it. The two limbs pull in different directions.

This limitation is in tension with the preceding sentence of Section 2.02(j), which states without qualification that the Insurer has all rights provided to it in the Operative Documents, of which the Indenture is one.

The deeming rule turns notice of a claim based on a mere "alleged violation" of the Truth-in-Lending Act into conclusive notice of an actual breach of a representation, so it is contestable whether an unfounded mortgagor claim triggers the repurchase machinery. "[C]onclusively constitute notice" also does not say whether the breach itself, as opposed to notice of it, is established.

The provision operates on Section 7 of the Depositor Purchase Agreement "as incorporated by reference into the Sale and Servicing Agreement," and its fit with Section 2.01(n), which imports all Operative Document representations directly for the Insurer's benefit, is unclear.

"Any such breach shall be deemed material and the remedies provided in Section 7 of the Depositor Purchase Agreement shall apply, including ..." leaves open whether those remedies are the exclusive consequence or merely additional, and the word "including" before the repurchase and indemnity obligations makes the list non-exhaustive. The indemnity's reach — "all losses, damages, claims and liabilities" — is stated in general terms after specific cost items.

The one-sentence covenant is in the passive voice and names no obligor, and it speaks of "Mortgage Loans" while the rest of the Agreement consistently uses "HELOCs." Whether the two terms are coextensive determines what is covered.
Neither "Mortgage Loans" nor its relation to the defined subject-matter "HELOCs" (used throughout the recitals and Sections 2.01 and 2.02) is settled anywhere in this Agreement.

The prohibition bites on any action or inaction that "may result in a Material Adverse Change," a possibility standard with no threshold, so almost any business decision could be argued to breach it. "[I]nterfere in any material respect with the enforcement of any rights of the Insurer" is similarly unbounded.

Notice is due on "the earlier of" a fixed date and "promptly prior to the date of consummation of such action," which is not a date at all, so the earlier-of formula cannot be applied as written. "[P]romptly prior to" has no fixed content.

The prohibition on mergers and asset transfers is subject to the circular exception "except as provided in the Operative Documents or as permitted hereby," which does not identify any permitted transaction. The exception could swallow the covenant depending on what other documents allow.

"[B]ankruptcy remote entity" is not defined in this Agreement and has no fixed legal content, so the standard the Depositor and Issuer must maintain is unstated. The negative formulation ("shall not cause ... to fail to maintain") further obscures whether it imposes an affirmative duty.

The representation is expressly cut down to a "limited scope of disclosure" defined only by the fact that the Insurer "is not the registrant," so what disclosure the Insurer has actually warranted is left indeterminate. The qualifier is unique in the Agreement and has no measurable boundary.

The confidentiality undertaking is subject to an open-ended string of exceptions — information "requested by appropriate governmental authorities" or disclosure "as necessary to preserve its rights or security under or to enforce the Operative Documents" — whose scope is not fixed. Whether disclosure to reinsurers or rating agencies is an exception or a separate permission is also left to a proviso.

"[C]ommercially reasonable efforts" to obtain an accountants' consent letter is undefined and no benchmark is given for measuring the effort required. The clause also does not say what happens if the letter is not obtained.

"[T]he sole result of such breach shall be" the furnishing obligation operates as an exclusive-remedy clause, but it does not say whether it displaces damages or other remedies otherwise available for a breached representation. Sole-remedy language of this kind is a standard site of dispute.

The trigger refers to "the representation in Section 2.05(i)" no longer being true, but Section 2.05(i) contains a consent, not a representation; the representation is in Section 2.05(j). The mis-citation determines when the Insurer's obligation to furnish financial statements arises.
As written this clause cannot be squared with Section 2.05(j), which says the breach of the Section 2.05(j) representation is what triggers furnishing "pursuant to Section 2.05(k) below."

The trailing qualifier "without regard to affiliations by common control-with the Insurer" is obscure and appears to except from the representation the very category of affiliation most likely to exist. Whether it narrows or negates the no-affiliation statement is genuinely unclear.

The operative promise to issue the Policy "subject to satisfaction of the conditions precedent set forth below" points the other way from the recital that "the Insurer has issued the Policy, pursuant to which it has agreed to pay," which treats issuance as already accomplished. Whether any condition remains available to the Insurer turns on which prevails.

"[T]he initial nonrefundable payment of the Premium, if applicable" does not say when such a payment is applicable, so it cannot be told from the Agreement whether this condition ever operates. The amount is left entirely to the Premium Letter.

The condition assumes representations "dated the Closing Date," but Section 2.01 gives representations "as of the Closing Date" in part in future terms ("is, or shall become") and Section 2.04 states no date for the Servicer's representations at all.

This condition speaks of a Default that "shall have occurred," whereas the corresponding representation in Section 2.01(f) is limited to a Default that "has occurred and is continuing"; a cured Default would satisfy one and not the other.

"[T]he Seller" is not a defined term in this Agreement, whose parties are the Sponsor, Depositor, Issuer, Servicer, Master Servicer, Indenture Trustee and Insurer; the recitals use "seller" for both GreenPoint (under the Seller's Purchase Agreement) and the Sponsor (under the Sale and Servicing Agreement). Who is billed for periodic rating agency fees therefore cannot be determined from the words.
The clause allocates fees "directly allocable to the Certificates," while Section 3.01(h) and the Transaction as a whole concern ratings on the Notes; the Agreement nowhere reconciles the two.

The absolute statement that the Insurer never bears Rating Agency fees sits against the next sentence of Section 3.02(a), under which fees of "any other rating agency" are borne by the requesting party — which could be the Insurer.

The clause again allocates cost to "the Seller," an undefined party, and the substitution proviso turns on when a Rating Agency "is no longer rating the Certificates" rather than the Notes. Both terms leave the payer uncertain.

The sentence is garbled — fees "incurred by the Insurer in connection with the issuance of the Policy amounts and as described in the Premium Letter" — so it cannot be told whether the Premium Letter caps the amounts or merely describes them. The stray word "amounts" breaks the sense of the obligation.

"[F]ully earned by the Insurer as of the date of issuance" but "payable in periodic installments" leaves open whether the whole Premium is recoverable if the Notes are retired early. The two halves of the sentence are in tension on their face.

The 30/360 convention here differs from the "actual number of days elapsed over a year of 360 days" convention fixed for the Late Payment Rate in Section 1.01, and neither says which applies to premium paid late.
